claim: The most frequent genetic cause of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia is a G4C2 repeat expansion in the C9orf72 gene.
source: The most frequent genetic cause of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia is a G4C2 repeat expansion in the C9orf72 gene.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citations in the introduction (DeJesus-Hernandez et al., 2011; Renton et al., 2011).

claim: The G4C2 expansion gives rise to translation of aggregating dipeptide repeat (DPR) proteins, including poly-GA as the most abundant species.
source: This expansion gives rise to translation of aggregating dipeptide repeat (DPR) proteins, including poly-GA as the most abundant species.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature (Mackenzie et al., 2015; Mori et al., 2013c; Schludi et al., 2015) mentioned in the introduction.

claim: Cytoplasmic poly-GA aggregates, generated in the absence of G4C2 RNA, interfered with nucleocytoplasmic protein transport.
source: Cytoplasmic poly-GA aggregates, generated in the absence of G4C2 RNA, interfered with nucleocytoplasmic protein transport, but had little effect on cell viability.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4, demonstrating impaired nuclear transport of S-mApple and p65 in cells expressing NES-GA65-GFP.

claim: Cytoplasmic poly-GA aggregates had little effect on cell viability.
source: Cytoplasmic poly-GA aggregates, generated in the absence of G4C2 RNA, interfered with nucleocytoplasmic protein transport, but had little effect on cell viability.
evidence: This is supported by MTT viability assay data shown in Figure 2D, where NES-GA65-GFP expression did not significantly reduce cell viability.

claim: Nuclear poly-GA was more toxic than cytoplasmic poly-GA.
source: In contrast, nuclear poly-GA was more toxic, impairing nucleolar protein quality control and protein biosynthesis.
evidence: This is supported by MTT viability assay data in Figure 2D showing significantly reduced viability with NLS-GA65-GFP compared to NES-GA65-GFP.

claim: Nuclear poly-GA impaired nucleolar protein quality control.
source: In contrast, nuclear poly-GA was more toxic, impairing nucleolar protein quality control and protein biosynthesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2C showing that NLS-GA65-GFP prevented repartitioning of NLS-LS from nucleolus to nucleoplasm after heat stress recovery.

claim: Nuclear poly-GA impaired protein biosynthesis.
source: In contrast, nuclear poly-GA was more toxic, impairing nucleolar protein quality control and protein biosynthesis.
evidence: This is supported by OPP incorporation data in Figure 5D-E showing reduced protein synthesis in cells expressing NLS-GA65-GFP.

claim: Production of the G4C2 RNA strongly reduced viability independent of DPR translation.
source: Production of the G4C2 RNA strongly reduced viability independent of DPR translation and caused pronounced inhibition of nuclear mRNA export and protein biogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by viability data in Figure 6A showing that all G4C2 constructs (NES, NLS, and untargeted) markedly decreased cellular viability, and by the absence of detectable R-DPR production from G4C2 constructs (Figure 6B).

claim: G4C2 RNA caused pronounced inhibition of nuclear mRNA export.
source: Production of the G4C2 RNA strongly reduced viability independent of DPR translation and caused pronounced inhibition of nuclear mRNA export and protein biogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by FISH data in Figure 5A-B showing strong nuclear mRNA accumulation in cells expressing G4C2 constructs but not synthetic GA constructs.

claim: G4C2 RNA caused pronounced inhibition of protein biogenesis.
source: Production of the G4C2 RNA strongly reduced viability independent of DPR translation and caused pronounced inhibition of nuclear mRNA export and protein biogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by OPP incorporation data in Figure 5D-E showing dramatically reduced protein synthesis in cells expressing G4C2 constructs.

claim: The toxic effects of G4C2 RNA predominate in the cellular model used.
source: Thus, while the toxic effects of G4C2 RNA predominate in the cellular model used, DPRs exert additive effects that may contribute to pathology.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparative toxicity data showing G4C2 constructs are more toxic than synthetic GA constructs (Figure 6A) and the absence of detectable R-DPR production (Figure 6B).

claim: DPRs exert additive effects that may contribute to pathology.
source: Thus, while the toxic effects of G4C2 RNA predominate in the cellular model used, DPRs exert additive effects that may contribute to pathology.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observation that NLS-(G4C2)73-GFP (producing both RNA and nuclear poly-GA) was more toxic than NLS-GA65-GFP alone (Figure 6A), and that nuclear poly-GA impairs protein synthesis (Figure 5D-E).

claim: Mutant C9orf72 in patients suffering from ALS/FTD can have more than a thousand G4C2 repeats.
source: Mutant C9orf72 in patients suffering from ALS/FTD can have more than a thousand G4C2 repeats, while healthy individuals possess usually less than 20 repeats (Gijselinck et al., 2016; Nordin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Gijselinck et al., 2016; Nordin et al., 2015).

claim: Healthy individuals possess usually less than 20 G4C2 repeats.
source: Mutant C9orf72 in patients suffering from ALS/FTD can have more than a thousand G4C2 repeats, while healthy individuals possess usually less than 20 repeats (Gijselinck et al., 2016; Nordin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Gijselinck et al., 2016; Nordin et al., 2015).

claim: Transcripts with expanded G4C2 tracts are translated by repeat associated non-AUG (RAN) translation in all reading frames and in both strands.
source: Transcripts with expanded G4C2 tracts are translated by repeat associated non-AUG (RAN) translation in all reading frames and in both strands, resulting in the synthesis of five different dipeptide repeat proteins (DPRs): poly-GA, poly-GR, poly-GP, poly-PR, and poly-PA (Ash et al., 2013; Gendron et al., 2013; Mackenzie et al., 2015; Mori et al., 2013a; Mori et al., 2013c; Zu et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Ash et al., 2013; Gendron et al., 2013; Mackenzie et al., 2015; Mori et al., 2013a; Mori et al., 2013c; Zu et al., 2013).

claim: RAN translation of G4C2 transcripts results in the synthesis of five different dipeptide repeat proteins (DPRs): poly-GA, poly-GR, poly-GP, poly-PR, and poly-PA.
source: Transcripts with expanded G4C2 tracts are translated by repeat associated non-AUG (RAN) translation in all reading frames and in both strands, resulting in the synthesis of five different dipeptide repeat proteins (DPRs): poly-GA, poly-GR, poly-GP, poly-PR, and poly-PA (Ash et al., 2013; Gendron et al., 2013; Mackenzie et al., 2015; Mori et al., 2013a; Mori et al., 2013c; Zu et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Ash et al., 2013; Gendron et al., 2013; Mackenzie et al., 2015; Mori et al., 2013a; Mori et al., 2013c; Zu et al., 2013).

claim: All five DPRs have been detected in patient brains.
source: all of which have been detected in patient brains (Mori et al., 2013a; Mori et al., 2013c; Zu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Mori et al., 2013a; Mori et al., 2013c; Zu et al., 2013).

claim: Poly-GA is the most abundant of the DPRs, followed by the other sense strand-encoded forms (poly-GP and poly-GR).
source: Poly-GA is the most abundant of the DPRs, followed by the other sense strand-encoded forms (poly-GP and poly-GR) (Mackenzie et al., 2015; Mori et al., 2013c; Schludi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Mackenzie et al., 2015; Mori et al., 2013c; Schludi et al., 2015).

claim: DPRs accumulate in deposits that can be found in the nucleus and cytoplasm, including neurites.
source: In patient brain and cellular models, DPRs accumulate in deposits that can be found in the nucleus and cytoplasm, including neurites (Ash et al., 2013; Gendron et al., 2013; Mackenzie et al., 2015; Mori et al., 2013a; Mori et al., 2013c; Schludi et al., 2015; Zu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Ash et al., 2013; Gendron et al., 2013; Mackenzie et al., 2015; Mori et al., 2013a; Mori et al., 2013c; Schludi et al., 2015; Zu et al., 2013).

claim: Poly-GA aggregates are localized mainly in the cytoplasm.
source: Poly-GA aggregates are localized mainly in the cytoplasm (Davidson et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2017; Mackenzie et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations (Davidson et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2017; Mackenzie et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2016).

claim: Arginine-containing DPRs (R-DPRs; poly-GR and poly-PR) accumulate in the nucleus.
source: whereas arginine-containing DPRs (R-DPRs; poly-GR and poly-PR) accumulate in the nucleus (Mackenzie et al., 2015; Schludi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Mackenzie et al., 2015; Schludi et al., 2015).

claim: R-DPRs have been shown in cellular models to localize to the nucleolus.
source: R-DPRs have also been shown in cellular models to localize to the nucleolus (Kwon et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2017; May et al., 2014; Moens et al., 2019; Wen et al., 2014; White et al., 2019; Yamakawa et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Kwon et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2017; May et al., 2014; Moens et al., 2019; Wen et al., 2014; White et al., 2019; Yamakawa et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2014).

claim: In patients, poly-GR and poly-PR predominantly form cytoplasmic deposits, with only a fraction of cells containing para-nucleolar inclusions.
source: However, in patients, poly-GR and poly-PR predominantly form cytoplasmic deposits, with only a fraction of cells containing para-nucleolar inclusions that co-localize with silent DNA (Mackenzie et al., 2015; Schludi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Mackenzie et al., 2015; Schludi et al., 2015).

claim: The less frequent intranuclear poly-GA inclusions in both cell models and patient brain are excluded from the nucleoli.
source: Interestingly, the less frequent intranuclear poly-GA inclusions in both cell models and patient brain are excluded from the nucleoli (Schludi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Schludi et al., 2015) and confirmed by experimental data in Figure 2B showing NLS-GA65-GFP aggregates do not co-localize with RPA40.

claim: The G4C2 expansion can alter the expression level of the C9ORF72 protein.
source: Despite its location in a non-coding part of the gene, the G4C2 expansion can alter the expression level of the C9ORF72 protein (Rizzu et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2018; Waite et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Rizzu et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2018; Waite et al., 2014).

claim: C9orf72 knockout mouse models failed to fully recapitulate ALS- or FTD-related neurodegenerative phenotypes.
source: However, C9orf72 knockout mouse models failed to fully recapitulate ALS- or FTD-related neurodegenerative phenotypes, suggesting that loss of C9ORF72 protein is not the only contributor to pathology (Atanasio et al., 2016; Burberry et al., 2016; Burberry et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2016; Koppers et al., 2015; Lagier-Tourenne et al., 2013; O'Rourke et al., 2016; Panda et al., 2013; Sudria-Lopez et al., 2016; Sullivan et al., 2016; Suzuki et al., 2013; Ugolino et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Atanasio et al., 2016; Burberry et al., 2016; Burberry et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2016; Koppers et al., 2015; Lagier-Tourenne et al., 2013; O'Rourke et al., 2016; Panda et al., 2013; Sudria-Lopez et al., 2016; Sullivan et al., 2016; Suzuki et al., 2013; Ugolino et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2020).

claim: Loss of C9ORF72 protein is not the only contributor to pathology.
source: However, C9orf72 knockout mouse models failed to fully recapitulate ALS- or FTD-related neurodegenerative phenotypes, suggesting that loss of C9ORF72 protein is not the only contributor to pathology (Atanasio et al., 2016; Burberry et al., 2016; Burberry et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2016; Koppers et al., 2015; Lagier-Tourenne et al., 2013; O'Rourke et al., 2016; Panda et al., 2013; Sudria-Lopez et al., 2016; Sullivan et al., 2016; Suzuki et al., 2013; Ugolino et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited knockout studies showing incomplete phenotype recapitulation.

claim: Pathological G4C2 mRNA forms stable G-quadruplexes in the nucleus.
source: Pathological G4C2 mRNA forms stable G-quadruplexes in the nucleus that retain RNA binding proteins and induce splicing defects (Cooper-Knock et al., 2014; Donnelly et al., 2013; Gitler and Tsuiji, 2016; Haeusler et al., 2014; Sareen et al., 2013; Simón-Sánchez et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Cooper-Knock et al., 2014; Donnelly et al., 2013; Gitler and Tsuiji, 2016; Haeusler et al., 2014; Sareen et al., 2013; Simón-Sánchez et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2013).

claim: G4C2 mRNA G-quadruplexes retain RNA binding proteins and induce splicing defects.
source: Pathological G4C2 mRNA forms stable G-quadruplexes in the nucleus that retain RNA binding proteins and induce splicing defects (Cooper-Knock et al., 2014; Donnelly et al., 2013; Gitler and Tsuiji, 2016; Haeusler et al., 2014; Sareen et al., 2013; Simón-Sánchez et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Cooper-Knock et al., 2014; Donnelly et al., 2013; Gitler and Tsuiji, 2016; Haeusler et al., 2014; Sareen et al., 2013; Simón-Sánchez et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2013).

claim: G4C2 mRNA has been observed in the cytoplasm.
source: but has also been observed in the cytoplasm (Cooper-Knock et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2016; Mizielinska et al., 2017; Ohki et al., 2017; Swinnen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Cooper-Knock et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2016; Mizielinska et al., 2017; Ohki et al., 2017; Swinnen et al., 2018).

claim: G4C2-containing RNA and associated DPRs have been reported to alter the nucleocytoplasmic transport machinery.
source: G4C2-containing RNA and associated DPRs have been reported to alter the nucleocytoplasmic transport machinery (Boeynaems et al., 2016; Freibaum et al., 2015; Jovičić et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Boeynaems et al., 2016; Freibaum et al., 2015; Jovičić et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015).

claim: R-DPRs can interact with membrane-free phase-separated compartments, such as the nucleolus, causing nucleolar stress and dysfunction.
source: Moreover, R-DPRs can interact with membrane-free phase-separated compartments, such as the nucleolus, causing nucleolar stress and dysfunction of nucleolar quality control, impairment of nucleocytoplasmic trafficking and protein translation, as well as induction of stress granule formation (Frottin et al., 2019; Hayes et al., 2020; Kanekura et al., 2016; Kwon et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2016; Mizielinska et al., 2017; Moens et al., 2019; Radwan et al., 2020; Shi et al., 2017; Tao et al., 2015; Vanneste et al., 2019; White et al., 2019; Yamakawa et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Frottin et al., 2019; Hayes et al., 2020; Kanekura et al., 2016; Kwon et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2016; Mizielinska et al., 2017; Moens et al., 2019; Radwan et al., 2020; Shi et al., 2017; Tao et al., 2015; Vanneste et al., 2019; White et al., 2019; Yamakawa et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2018b).

claim: Cytoplasmic poly-GA aggregates associate extensively with proteasomes and other components of the ubiquitin proteasome system.
source: Additionally, cytoplasmic poly-GA aggregates associate extensively with proteasomes and other components of the ubiquitin proteasome system, and interfere with proteasome activity (Al-Sarraj et al., 2011; Guo et al., 2018; Khosravi et al., 2020; May et al., 2014; Mori et al., 2013c; Riemslagh et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations (Al-Sarraj et al., 2011; Guo et al., 2018; Khosravi et al., 2020; May et al., 2014; Mori et al., 2013c; Riemslagh et al., 2019).

claim: Cytoplasmic poly-GA aggregates interfere with proteasome activity.
source: Additionally, cytoplasmic poly-GA aggregates associate extensively with proteasomes and other components of the ubiquitin proteasome system, and interfere with proteasome activity (Al-Sarraj et al., 2011; Guo et al., 2018; Khosravi et al., 2020; May et al., 2014; Mori et al., 2013c; Riemslagh et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations (Al-Sarraj et al., 2011; Guo et al., 2018; Khosravi et al., 2020; May et al., 2014; Mori et al., 2013c; Riemslagh et al., 2019).

claim: Cytoplasmic poly-GA aggregates induce mislocalization of nuclear proteins.
source: as well as induce mislocalization of nuclear proteins (Khosravi et al., 2017; Nihei et al., 2020; Nonaka et al., 2018; Solomon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Khosravi et al., 2017; Nihei et al., 2020; Nonaka et al., 2018; Solomon et al., 2018).

claim: In mice expressing poly-GA, the aggregates have been observed to sequester nuclear pore components.
source: In mice expressing poly-GA, the aggregates have also been observed to sequester nuclear pore components (Zhang et al., 2016), thereby interfering with nucleocytoplasmic protein transport.
evidence: This is supported by citation (Zhang et al., 2016).

claim: Expression of GA65-GFP in HEK293 cells resulted in the formation of bright fluorescent inclusions in most transfected cells.
source: Expression of GA65-GFP in HEK293 cells resulted in the formation of bright fluorescent inclusions in most transfected cells.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 1B showing GA65-GFP inclusions.

claim: GA65-GFP inclusions were generally cytoplasmic, except for a small fraction of cells with nuclear foci.
source: The inclusions were generally cytoplasmic, except for a small fraction of cells with nuclear foci (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 1B.

claim: The localization of GA65-GFP aggregates is consistent with reports on the localization of poly-GA aggregates in patient brain.
source: This phenotype is consistent with reports on the localization of poly-GA aggregates in patient brain, where poly-GA aggregates are also observed in the neuronal cytoplasm and nucleus (Mori et al., 2013c; Schludi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference comparing experimental observations with cited literature (Mori et al., 2013c; Schludi et al., 2015).

claim: NES-GA65-GFP accumulated in the cytoplasm and formed inclusions similar to those of GA65-GFP.
source: NES-GA65-GFP accumulated in the cytoplasm and formed inclusions similar to those of GA65-GFP (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 1B.

claim: Directing poly-GA to the nucleus with NLS resulted in an increased number of cells with nuclear aggregates.
source: Directing the protein to the nucleus resulted in an increased number of cells with nuclear aggregates (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 1B showing NLS-GA65-GFP nuclear aggregates.

claim: A number of NLS-GA65-GFP-expressing cells also contained cytoplasmic inclusions.
source: However, a number of NLS-GA65-GFP-expressing cells also contained cytoplasmic inclusions, suggesting that aggregate formation in these cells occurred before the transport of the poly-GA proteins into the nucleus.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 1B and is an inference about the timing of aggregation.

claim: Poly-GA forms p62-positive inclusions in the cytoplasm of neurons.
source: Poly-GA forms p62-positive inclusions in the cytoplasm of neurons (Guo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Guo et al., 2018).

claim: p62-positive poly-GA inclusions of GA65-GFP and NES-GA65-GFP were observed in HEK293 cells.
source: We were able to replicate this phenotype in our cellular system and observed p62-positive poly-GA inclusions of GA65-GFP and NES-GA65-GFP (Figure 1C; May et al., 2014; Mori et al., 2013c).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 1C and citations (May et al., 2014; Mori et al., 2013c).

claim: Both nuclear and cytoplasmic poly-GA inclusions were stained throughout with AmyT, a small amyloid-specific dye.
source: Both nuclear and cytoplasmic poly-GA inclusions were stained throughout with AmyT, a small amyloid-specific dye (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 1D showing AmyT staining.

claim: Poly-GA aggregates were recognized by the anti-amyloid antibody (OC).
source: The aggregates were also recognized by the anti-amyloid antibody (OC) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), which recognizes generic epitopes common to amyloid fibrils and fibrillar oligomers (Kayed et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and citation (Kayed et al., 2007).

claim: Nuclear aggregates stained homogeneously with OC, while cytoplasmic GA65-GFP inclusions showed only peripheral reaction with the dye.
source: However, while the nuclear aggregates stained homogeneously with OC, cytoplasmic GA65-GFP inclusions stained less well and rather showed only a peripheral reaction with the dye (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The differential antibody accessibility of the inclusion core suggests that the nuclear and cytoplasmic DPR aggregates differ in structural properties such as packing density.
source: The differential antibody accessibility of the inclusion core suggests that the nuclear and cytoplasmic DPR aggregates, though both amyloid-like, differ in structural properties such as packing density.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential OC staining patterns observed in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: NES-GA65-GFP was retained in a filter retardation assay in the presence of SDS.
source: NES-GA65-GFP was retained in a filter retardation assay in the presence of SDS, while most NLS-GA65-GFP passed through the filter (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by filter retardation assay data in Figure 1E.

claim: Most NLS-GA65-GFP passed through the filter in a filter retardation assay.
source: NES-GA65-GFP was retained in a filter retardation assay in the presence of SDS, while most NLS-GA65-GFP passed through the filter (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by filter retardation assay data in Figure 1E.

claim: The difference in detergent solubility was not due to the presence of the NLS sequence.
source: The difference in detergent solubility was not due to the presence of the NLS sequence since similar results were obtained using the FUS-derived C-terminal nuclear localization signal (PY) (Gal et al., 2011; Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by filter retardation assay data in Figure 1E comparing NLS and PY constructs, and citation (Gal et al., 2011).

claim: Disabling of the nuclear targeting sequences by point mutations resulted in the reappearance of SDS-insoluble aggregates.
source: Moreover, disabling of the nuclear targeting sequences by point mutations resulted in the reappearance of SDS-insoluble aggregates (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by filter retardation assay data in Figure 1E showing mutant constructs.

claim: Nuclear and cytoplasmic poly-GA aggregates have different physico-chemical properties despite being amyloid-like.
source: Thus, despite being amyloid-like, nuclear and cytoplasmic poly-GA aggregates have different physico-chemical properties.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential solubility (Figure 1E) and antibody staining patterns (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).

claim: The granular component (GC) of the nucleolus functions as a protein quality control compartment.
source: The granular component (GC) of the nucleolus has recently been shown to function as a protein quality control compartment (Frottin et al., 2019; Woerner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Frottin et al., 2019; Woerner et al., 2016).

claim: Nuclear aggregates of NLS-GA65-GFP altered the localization of the GC marker protein nucleophosmin (NPM1).
source: Interestingly, the nuclear aggregates of NLS-GA65-GFP altered the localization of the GC marker protein nucleophosmin (NPM1), while cytosolic NES-GA65-GFP had no such effect (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 2A showing NPM1 mislocalization with NLS-GA65-GFP but not NES-GA65-GFP.

claim: Cytosolic NES-GA65-GFP had no effect on NPM1 localization.
source: Interestingly, the nuclear aggregates of NLS-GA65-GFP altered the localization of the GC marker protein nucleophosmin (NPM1), while cytosolic NES-GA65-GFP had no such effect (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 2A.

claim: Nuclear GA65-GFP aggregates induced the dislocation of NPM1 from the GC phase of the nucleolus, with accumulation of NPM1 at the aggregate periphery.
source: Nuclear GA65-GFP aggregates induced the dislocation of NPM1 from the GC phase of the nucleolus, with accumulation of NPM1 at the aggregate periphery (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 2A showing NPM1 accumulation at aggregate periphery.

claim: Nuclear GA65-GFP deposits did not alter the distribution of the RNA polymerase I subunit RPA40.
source: However, the nuclear GA65-GFP deposits did not alter the distribution of the RNA polymerase I subunit RPA40, a marker of the fibrillar center of the nucleolus, the site of rRNA synthesis (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 2B showing normal RPA40 distribution.

claim: The NPM1-containing GC phase is responsible for pre-ribosome particle assembly.
source: The NPM1-containing GC phase is responsible for pre-ribosome particle assembly and also accommodates proteins that have misfolded upon stress.
evidence: This is established knowledge about nucleolar function.

claim: The GC phase accommodates proteins that have misfolded upon stress and maintains them in a state competent for refolding.
source: The NPM1-containing GC phase is responsible for pre-ribosome particle assembly and also accommodates proteins that have misfolded upon stress. These proteins enter the GC phase and are maintained in a state competent for refolding and repartitioning to the nucleoplasm upon recovery from stress (Frottin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Frottin et al., 2019).

claim: R-DPRs enter the GC phase of the nucleolus and convert it from liquid-like to a more hardened state.
source: In contrast to poly-GA, R-DPRs enter the GC phase of the nucleolus and convert it from liquid-like to a more hardened state, thereby impairing its quality control function (Frottin et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Frottin et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2016).

claim: In control cells, NLS-LS accumulated in the nucleolus upon heat stress and largely repartitioned to the nucleoplasm within 2 hr of recovery.
source: In control cells, NLS-LS accumulated in the nucleolus upon heat stress and largely repartitioned to the nucleoplasm within 2 hr of recovery (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images and quantification in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Expression of cytoplasmic NES-GA65-GFP did not affect NLS-LS repartitioning after heat stress recovery.
source: A similar result was obtained upon expression of cytoplasmic NES-GA65-GFP.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2C showing similar repartitioning with NES-GA65-GFP as control.

claim: In the presence of aggregates of NLS-GA65-GFP, NLS-LS failed to efficiently repartition to the nucleoplasm.
source: However, in the presence of aggregates of NLS-GA65-GFP, NLS-LS failed to efficiently repartition to the nucleoplasm (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), indicating that the nuclear poly-GA aggregates compromise nucleolar protein quality control.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images and quantification in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Nuclear poly-GA aggregates compromise nucleolar protein quality control.
source: However, in the presence of aggregates of NLS-GA65-GFP, NLS-LS failed to efficiently repartition to the nucleoplasm (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), indicating that the nuclear poly-GA aggregates compromise nucleolar protein quality control.
evidence: This is an inference based on the NLS-LS repartitioning data in Figure 2C.

claim: Expression of NLS-GA65-GFP significantly reduced metabolic activity compared to NES-GA65-GFP.
source: While the expression of NES-GA65-GFP did not cause toxicity, metabolic activity was significantly reduced upon expression of NLS-GA65-GFP (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by MTT viability assay data in Figure 2D.

claim: The toxic effect of NLS-GA65-GFP was reproduced with an alternative degenerated and G4C2-free DNA sequence (GA65(2)).
source: This effect was reproduced in cells transfected with a plasmid coding for GA65 from an alternative degenerated and G4C2-free DNA sequence (GA65(2)) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), further excluding RNA-mediated toxicity.
evidence: This is supported by viability data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Decreased viability was observed when GA65-GFP was targeted to the nucleus via the alternative PY localization signal.
source: Decreased viability was also observed when GA65-GFP was targeted to the nucleus via the alternative PY localization signal (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by viability data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Both NES-GA65-GFP and NLS-GA65-GFP were expressed at levels comparable to GA65-GFP.
source: Importantly, both NES-GA65-GFP and NLS-GA65-GFP were expressed at levels comparable to GA65-GFP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Point mutations in the NLS or PY targeting sequence prevented accumulation of GA65-GFP in the nucleus and restored viability.
source: Point mutations in the NLS or PY targeting sequence prevented accumulation of GA65-GFP in the nucleus and restored viability (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by viability data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The difference in toxicity between nuclear and cytoplasmic poly-GA is caused by compartment-specific properties of the aggregates independent of their targeting sequences and mRNA.
source: Together, these results indicate that the difference in toxicity between nuclear and cytoplasmic poly-GA is caused by compartment-specific properties of the aggregates independent of their targeting sequences and mRNA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data from viability assays with different targeting sequences and mutations (Figures 2D, 2—figure supplement 1B-C).

claim: Artificial β-sheet proteins, when aggregating in the cytoplasm, sequester nuclear transport factors and interfere with transport of proteins and mRNA across the nuclear envelope.
source: We have previously shown that artificial β-sheet proteins, when aggregating in the cytoplasm, sequester nuclear transport factors and thereby interfere with transport of proteins and mRNA across the nuclear envelope (Woerner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Woerner et al., 2016).

claim: Similar observations of nuclear transport interference were made for the aggregates of various disease proteins including poly-GA and R-DPRs.
source: Similar observations were made for the aggregates of various disease proteins including poly-GA and R-DPRs (Boeynaems et al., 2016; Chou et al., 2018; Eftekharzadeh et al., 2019; Freibaum et al., 2015; Gasset-Rosa et al., 2017; Grima et al., 2017; Jovičić et al., 2015; Khosravi et al., 2017; Kramer et al., 2018; Solomon et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Boeynaems et al., 2016; Chou et al., 2018; Eftekharzadeh et al., 2019; Freibaum et al., 2015; Gasset-Rosa et al., 2017; Grima et al., 2017; Jovičić et al., 2015; Khosravi et al., 2017; Kramer et al., 2018; Solomon et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2016).

claim: At steady state, S-mApple localized mainly to the cytoplasm.
source: At steady state, S-mApple localized mainly to the cytoplasm, but accumulated within minutes in the nucleus upon inhibition of nuclear export with leptomycin B (LMB) (Wolff et al., 1997; Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 3A and citation (Wolff et al., 1997).

claim: S-mApple accumulated within minutes in the nucleus upon inhibition of nuclear export with leptomycin B (LMB).
source: At steady state, S-mApple localized mainly to the cytoplasm, but accumulated within minutes in the nucleus upon inhibition of nuclear export with leptomycin B (LMB) (Wolff et al., 1997; Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 3A and citation (Wolff et al., 1997).

claim: S-mApple was retained within the nucleus upon expression of the cytoplasmic β-sheet protein NES-β17.
source: As previously described, S-mApple was retained within the nucleus upon expression of the cytoplasmic β-sheet protein NES-β17 (Figure 3), indicative of inhibition of nuclear protein export (Woerner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images and quantification in Figure 3 and citation (Woerner et al., 2016).

claim: Expression of NES-GA65-GFP impaired S-mApple export from the nucleus, but to a lesser extent than NES-β17.
source: Expression of NES-GA65-GFP also impaired S-mApple export from the nucleus (-LMB), but to a lesser extent than NES-β17 (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images and quantification in Figure 3.

claim: NES-GA65-GFP caused a mild impairment of nuclear protein import.
source: A mild impairment of nuclear protein import by NES-GA65-GFP was also observed, as measured upon inhibition of export with LMB (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images and quantification in Figure 3B showing S-mApple distribution with LMB treatment.

claim: Nuclear poly-GA aggregates had only a weak effect on protein export.
source: As for NLS-β17, nuclear poly-GA aggregates had only a weak effect on protein export (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images and quantification in Figure 3.

claim: Cells containing nuclear aggregates did not show a significant change in S-mApple import into the nucleus.
source: Similarly, cells containing nuclear aggregates did not show a significant change in S-mApple import into the nucleus (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images and quantification in Figure 3B.

claim: In control cells, p65 is largely cytoplasmic and enters the nucleus upon treatment with TNFα.
source: In control cells, p65 is largely cytoplasmic and enters the nucleus upon treatment with TNFα (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images and quantification in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Cells containing NES-GA65-GFP aggregates displayed a potent inhibition of p65 translocation.
source: Cells containing NES-GA65-GFP aggregates displayed a potent inhibition of p65 translocation (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images and quantification in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Cytoplasmic aggregates of polyQ-expanded Huntingtin-exon 1 (Htt96Q) inhibited p65 translocation.
source: A similar effect was seen with cytoplasmic aggregates of polyQ-expanded Huntingtin-exon 1 (Htt96Q) as a positive control (Figure 4A, B; Woerner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images and quantification in Figure 4A-B and citation (Woerner et al., 2016).

claim: Cells containing cytoplasmic aggregates of untargeted GA65-GFP displayed reduced p65 translocation.
source: Cells containing cytoplasmic aggregates of untargeted GA65-GFP also displayed reduced p65 translocation (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images and quantification in Figure 4A-B.

claim: The observed p65 translocation impairment was independent of an alteration of p65 phosphorylation and degradation of IκB.
source: The observed translocation impairment was independent of an alteration of p65 phosphorylation and degradation of the inhibitor of nuclear factor κB (IκB) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 4C showing normal p65 phosphorylation and IκB degradation.

claim: Nuclear poly-GA aggregates showed only a limited effect on p65 translocation.
source: In contrast, nuclear poly-GA aggregates showed only a limited effect on p65 translocation (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images and quantification in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Cytoplasmic aggregates of β-sheet model proteins and disease-linked, amyloidogenic proteins cause mislocalization and sequestration of nuclear pore complexes and importins.
source: Cytoplasmic aggregates of β-sheet model proteins and disease-linked, amyloidogenic proteins cause mislocalization and sequestration of nuclear pore complexes and importins (Woerner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Woerner et al., 2016).

claim: R-DPRs directly bind and interfere with cargo loading onto importin β at the nuclear pore.
source: Particularly, R-DPRs have also been shown to directly bind and interfere with cargo loading onto importin β at the nuclear pore (Hayes et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Hayes et al., 2020).

claim: Cytoplasmic poly-GA aggregates had no apparent effect on the localization of the nuclear pore complex.
source: While cytoplasmic poly-GA aggregates had no apparent effect on the localization of the nuclear pore complex (Figure 1B)
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 1B showing normal NPC staining.

claim: Cells with cytoplasmic GA65-GFP aggregates frequently contained aggregate foci of importins α1 (KPNA2) and α3 (KPNA4).
source: we found that cells with cytoplasmic GA65-GFP aggregates frequently contained aggregate foci of importins α1 (KPNA2) and α3 (KPNA4), as has been observed previously for cytoplasmic aggregates of the aggregation-prone model proteins NES-β23 (Woerner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B and citation (Woerner et al., 2016).

claim: Importin β1 (KPNB1) aggregation was observed with cytoplasmic poly-GA, although to a lesser degree than importins α.
source: This effect was also observed for importin β1 (KPNB1), although to a lesser degree (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Importins appeared to be enriched at the periphery of poly-GA inclusions.
source: Additionally, importins appeared to be enriched at the periphery of poly-GA inclusions, as seen for KPNA2 and KPNA4 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images and fluorescence profiles in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Nuclear poly-GA aggregates had no effect on the distribution of importins.
source: Nuclear poly-GA aggregates had no effect on the distribution of these importins (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: An aberrant distribution of mRNA has been observed in mouse motor neuron-like cells expressing expanded G4C2 repeats and in C9orf72 patient cortical neurons.
source: An aberrant distribution of mRNA has been observed in mouse motor neuron-like cells expressing expanded G4C2 repeats and in C9orf72 patient cortical neurons (Freibaum et al., 2015; Rossi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Freibaum et al., 2015; Rossi et al., 2015).

claim: In control cells, mRNA was present throughout the cytoplasm and in small nuclear ribonucleic particles.
source: In control cells, mRNA was present throughout the cytoplasm and in small nuclear ribonucleic particles (Figure 5A; Carter et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by FISH images in Figure 5A and citation (Carter et al., 1991).

claim: Expression of NES-GA65-GFP had only a minor effect on cellular mRNA distribution.
source: Expression of NES-GA65-GFP had only a minor effect on cellular mRNA distribution (Figure 5A, B)
evidence: This is supported by FISH images and quantification in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Expression of cytoplasmic β-protein (NES-β17) resulted in pronounced nuclear mRNA retention.
source: in contrast to the expression of cytoplasmic β-protein (NES-β17), which resulted in pronounced nuclear mRNA retention (Woerner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by FISH images and quantification in Figure 5A-B and citation (Woerner et al., 2016).

claim: NLS-GA65-GFP only caused limited mRNA retention in the nucleus.
source: Likewise, NLS-GA65-GFP only caused limited mRNA retention in the nucleus (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This is supported by FISH images and quantification in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Poly-GA aggregates interfere with the function of only a subset of nuclear transport factors.
source: Thus, poly-GA aggregates interfere with the function of only a subset of nuclear transport factors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects on protein transport (Figures 3-4) versus mRNA export (Figure 5A-B).

claim: Both NES-(G4C2)73-GFP and NLS-(G4C2)73-GFP resulted in the formation of G4C2-positive RNA foci in the nucleus.
source: Both NES-(G4C2)73-GFP and NLS-(G4C2)73-GFP, besides generating DPR inclusions, resulted in the formation of G4C2-positive RNA foci in the nucleus, as observed by fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) using a C4G2 probe (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by FISH images in Figure 5C.

claim: Only the G4C2 constructs showed mRNA accumulation in the nucleus of the majority of cells.
source: Cells expressing GA65-GFP or (G4C2)73-GFP without targeting sequence were analyzed as well, but only the G4C2 constructs showed mRNA accumulation in the nucleus of the majority of cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by FISH images and quantification in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: G4C2 RNA foci are associated with nuclear mRNA accumulation, independent of the presence of visible poly-GA protein aggregates.
source: Furthermore, simultaneous visualization of G4C2 RNA puncta with the C4G2 probe, total mRNA using an oligo-dT probe and GA-GFP revealed that the G4C2 RNA foci are associated with nuclear mRNA accumulation, independent of the presence of visible poly-GA protein aggregates (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by FISH images and quantification in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: G4C2 RNA, not poly-GA protein, mediates retention of mRNA in the nucleus.
source: Together, these results indicate that G4C2 RNA, not poly-GA protein, mediates retention of mRNA in the nucleus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential mRNA retention between synthetic GA and G4C2 constructs (Figures 5A-B, 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: Nuclear mRNA retention in cells expressing G4C2 constructs was accompanied by a marked reduction of protein synthesis.
source: The nuclear mRNA retention in cells expressing G4C2 constructs was accompanied by a marked reduction of protein synthesis as measured by the incorporation of a puromycin derivative into newly translated proteins (Slomnicki et al., 2016; Figure 5D, E).
evidence: This is supported by OPP incorporation data in Figure 5D-E and citation (Slomnicki et al., 2016).

claim: NLS-GA65-GFP-expressing cells displayed reduced protein synthesis, independently of G4C2 RNA.
source: Interestingly, NLS-GA65-GFP-expressing cells also displayed reduced protein synthesis, independently of G4C2 RNA.
evidence: This is supported by OPP incorporation data in Figure 5D-E.

claim: NES-GA65-GFP had no inhibitory effect on protein synthesis.
source: In contrast, NES-GA65-GFP had no inhibitory effect on protein synthesis (Figure 5D, E).
evidence: This is supported by OPP incorporation data in Figure 5D-E.

claim: Cells expressing NLS-(G4C2)73-GFP were almost completely translation inactive.
source: Notably, cells expressing NLS-(G4C2)73-GFP, accumulating both nuclear poly-GA protein and G4C2 RNA, were almost completely translation inactive, similar to control cells treated with the translation inhibitor cycloheximide (Figure 5D, E).
evidence: This is supported by OPP incorporation data in Figure 5D-E.

claim: Nuclear poly-GA protein and G4C2 RNA have additive inhibitory effects on protein biosynthesis.
source: Thus, both nuclear poly-GA protein and G4C2 RNA appear to have additive inhibitory effects on protein biosynthesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that NLS-(G4C2)73-GFP (with both RNA and nuclear poly-GA) shows greater inhibition than either NLS-GA65-GFP or NES-(G4C2)73-GFP alone (Figure 5D-E).

claim: Independent of the presence of a NES or NLS targeting sequence, all G4C2 constructs markedly decreased cellular viability.
source: Independent of the presence of a NES or NLS targeting sequence, all G4C2 constructs markedly decreased cellular viability (Figure 6A), indicating that toxicity was mediated by the expanded G4C2 RNA.
evidence: This is supported by viability data in Figure 6A.

claim: Toxicity of G4C2 constructs was mediated by the expanded G4C2 RNA.
source: Independent of the presence of a NES or NLS targeting sequence, all G4C2 constructs markedly decreased cellular viability (Figure 6A), indicating that toxicity was mediated by the expanded G4C2 RNA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that all G4C2 constructs (regardless of DPR localization) were toxic (Figure 6A).

claim: Expression of NLS-(G4C2)73-GFP was more toxic than NLS-GA65-GFP.
source: Moreover, expression of NLS-(G4C2)73-GFP was more toxic than NLS-GA65-GFP (Figure 6A), although the poly-GA levels of the constructs were comparable (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by viability data in Figure 6A and expression level data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The poly-GA levels of NLS-(G4C2)73-GFP and NLS-GA65-GFP constructs were comparable.
source: Moreover, expression of NLS-(G4C2)73-GFP was more toxic than NLS-GA65-GFP (Figure 6A), although the poly-GA levels of the constructs were comparable (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GR73-GFP was located predominantly within the cytoplasm and the nucleolus of HEK293 cells.
source: GR73-GFP was located predominantly within the cytoplasm and the nucleolus of HEK293 cells, while PR73-GFP accumulated within the nucleoplasm and nucleolus (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), as reported previously (Frottin et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2016; May et al., 2014; White et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and citations (Frottin et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2016; May et al., 2014; White et al., 2019).

claim: PR73-GFP accumulated within the nucleoplasm and nucleolus.
source: GR73-GFP was located predominantly within the cytoplasm and the nucleolus of HEK293 cells, while PR73-GFP accumulated within the nucleoplasm and nucleolus (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), as reported previously (Frottin et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2016; May et al., 2014; White et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and citations (Frottin et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2016; May et al., 2014; White et al., 2019).

claim: Expression of (G4C2)73-GFP dramatically reduced cellular viability.
source: While the expression of (G4C2)73-GFP dramatically reduced cellular viability, the R-DPRs were not measurably cytotoxic (Figure 6A)
evidence: This is supported by viability data in Figure 6A.

claim: R-DPRs (PR73-GFP and GR73-GFP) were not measurably cytotoxic.
source: While the expression of (G4C2)73-GFP dramatically reduced cellular viability, the R-DPRs were not measurably cytotoxic (Figure 6A), consistent with an earlier report for constructs with longer repeat lengths (May et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by viability data in Figure 6A and citation (May et al., 2014).

claim: Anti-GR and anti-PR antibodies recognized specific signals in cells transfected with the respective R-DPR constructs.
source: The antibodies recognized specific signals in cells transfected with the respective R-DPR constructs, but failed to detect R-DPR protein in cells expressing (G4C2)73-GFP (Figure 6B)
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 6B.

claim: Anti-GR and anti-PR antibodies failed to detect R-DPR protein in cells expressing (G4C2)73-GFP.
source: The antibodies recognized specific signals in cells transfected with the respective R-DPR constructs, but failed to detect R-DPR protein in cells expressing (G4C2)73-GFP (Figure 6B), indicating that production of R-DPR protein from the G4C2 constructs was very inefficient.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 6B.

claim: Production of R-DPR protein from the G4C2 constructs was very inefficient.
source: The antibodies recognized specific signals in cells transfected with the respective R-DPR constructs, but failed to detect R-DPR protein in cells expressing (G4C2)73-GFP (Figure 6B), indicating that production of R-DPR protein from the G4C2 constructs was very inefficient.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of detectable R-DPR signal in (G4C2)73-GFP samples (Figure 6B).

claim: The pronounced toxicity observed upon expression of (G4C2)73-GFP cannot be explained by RAN translation of R-DPR but is due to nuclear mRNA retention mediated by the G4C2 repeat RNA.
source: Given that PR73-GFP and GR73-GFP were produced in detectable quantities from the synthetic constructs without inducing toxicity, we conclude that the pronounced toxicity observed upon expression of (G4C2)73-GFP cannot be explained by RAN translation of R-DPR but is due to nuclear mRNA retention mediated by the G4C2 repeat RNA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined observations that R-DPRs alone are not toxic (Figure 6A), R-DPRs are not detectably produced from G4C2 constructs (Figure 6B), and G4C2 constructs cause mRNA retention (Figure 5A-B).

claim: The G4C2 expansion causes toxicity in a manner dependent on both aggregates of G4C2-encoded DPR proteins and the G4C2 repeat mRNA.
source: Our results demonstrated that the G4C2 expansion causes toxicity in our cellular system in a manner dependent on both aggregates of G4C2-encoded DPR proteins and the G4C2 repeat mRNA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined toxicity data showing both nuclear poly-GA (Figure 2D) and G4C2 RNA (Figure 6A) contribute to toxicity.

claim: The findings suggest a multiple hit model of additive, but mechanistically independent, effects of proteotoxicity and RNA-mediated toxicity.
source: These findings suggest a multiple hit model of additive, but mechanistically independent, effects of proteotoxicity and RNA-mediated toxicity, with the latter being the predominant toxic agent in the model system investigated.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observation that different toxic mechanisms operate independently (protein transport, mRNA export, protein synthesis) and have additive effects.

claim: RNA-mediated toxicity is the predominant toxic agent in the model system investigated.
source: These findings suggest a multiple hit model of additive, but mechanistically independent, effects of proteotoxicity and RNA-mediated toxicity, with the latter being the predominant toxic agent in the model system investigated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the greater toxicity of G4C2 constructs compared to synthetic GA constructs (Figure 6A).

claim: The longer G4C2 expansions, and the resulting DPRs, present in patients may have additional adverse effects that were not recapitulated with the constructs used in this study.
source: However, the longer G4C2 expansions, and the resulting DPRs, present in patients may have additional adverse effects that were not recapitulated with the constructs used here.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning acknowledging limitations of the model system.

claim: Both DPRs and repeat mRNA interfered with different aspects of nucleocytoplasmic transport.
source: Both DPRs and repeat mRNA interfered with different aspects of nucleocytoplasmic transport.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on data showing poly-GA affects protein transport (Figures 3-4) while G4C2 RNA affects mRNA export (Figure 5A-B).

claim: The G4C2 RNA inhibited the export of mRNA from the nucleus.
source: The G4C2 RNA inhibited the export of mRNA from the nucleus, consistent with a dramatic impairment of protein synthesis that would be associated with strong neuronal toxicity.
evidence: This is supported by FISH data in Figure 5A-B showing nuclear mRNA accumulation with G4C2 constructs.

claim: G4C2 RNA-mediated mRNA export inhibition is consistent with a dramatic impairment of protein synthesis that would be associated with strong neuronal toxicity.
source: The G4C2 RNA inhibited the export of mRNA from the nucleus, consistent with a dramatic impairment of protein synthesis that would be associated with strong neuronal toxicity.
evidence: This is an inference connecting mRNA retention to protein synthesis defects and speculating about neuronal consequences.

claim: The mRNA export inhibition effect of G4C2 RNA was independent of the presence of DPR protein aggregates.
source: Notably, this effect was independent of the presence of DPR protein aggregates, which is in agreement with results from zebrafish (Swinnen et al., 2018), but in contrast to findings observed in Drosophila (Tran et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B showing mRNA retention with G4C2 RNA foci independent of visible aggregates, and citations (Swinnen et al., 2018; Tran et al., 2015).

claim: Cytoplasmic poly-GA aggregates partially inhibited the transport of proteins across the nuclear pore.
source: Additionally, as has been reported for artificial β-sheet proteins and disease-associated aggregation-prone proteins such as Tau, Huntingtin, FUS, and TDP-43 (Chou et al., 2018; Dormann et al., 2010; Eftekharzadeh et al., 2019; Gasset-Rosa et al., 2017; Grima et al., 2017; Woerner et al., 2016), cytoplasmic poly-GA aggregates partially inhibited the transport of proteins across the nuclear pore.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 3-4 and citations (Chou et al., 2018; Dormann et al., 2010; Eftekharzadeh et al., 2019; Gasset-Rosa et al., 2017; Grima et al., 2017; Woerner et al., 2016).

claim: The observation of nuclear transport inhibition by cytoplasmic poly-GA is in agreement with the previously reported sequestration of a subset of transport factors by poly-GA.
source: This observation is in agreement with the previously reported sequestration of a subset of transport factors by poly-GA (Khosravi et al., 2017; Solomon et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2016), and the importin pathology that has been observed in postmortem frontal cortex tissue of ALS/FTD C9orf72 patients (Solomon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference connecting experimental observations with cited literature (Khosravi et al., 2017; Solomon et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2016).

claim: Importin pathology has been observed in postmortem frontal cortex tissue of ALS/FTD C9orf72 patients.
source: This observation is in agreement with the previously reported sequestration of a subset of transport factors by poly-GA (Khosravi et al., 2017; Solomon et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2016), and the importin pathology that has been observed in postmortem frontal cortex tissue of ALS/FTD C9orf72 patients (Solomon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Solomon et al., 2018).

claim: Other DPRs have been reported to inhibit additional aspects of nucleocytoplasmic transport.
source: Interestingly, other DPRs have also been reported to inhibit additional aspects of nucleocytoplasmic transport (Boeynaems et al., 2017; Cook et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Boeynaems et al., 2017; Cook et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018a).

claim: Poly-PR can directly obstruct the central channel of the nuclear pore by binding to the FG domains of nuclear pore proteins.
source: Poly-PR can directly obstruct the central channel of the nuclear pore by binding to the FG domains of nuclear pore proteins (Shi et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citation (Shi et al., 2017).

claim: R-DPRs can disrupt cargo loading onto karyopherins β.
source: and R-DPRs can disrupt cargo loading onto karyopherins β (Hayes et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Hayes et al., 2020).

claim: The effects of cytoplasmic poly-GA (NES-poly-GA) aggregates on nuclear transport were well tolerated in the cell culture model.
source: While the effects of cytoplasmic poly-GA (NES-poly-GA) aggregates on nuclear transport were well tolerated in our cell culture model, poly-GA aggregates within the nucleus (NLS-poly-GA) were associated with substantial proteotoxicity.
evidence: This is supported by viability data in Figure 2D showing no toxicity with NES-GA65-GFP.

claim: Poly-GA aggregates within the nucleus (NLS-poly-GA) were associated with substantial proteotoxicity.
source: While the effects of cytoplasmic poly-GA (NES-poly-GA) aggregates on nuclear transport were well tolerated in our cell culture model, poly-GA aggregates within the nucleus (NLS-poly-GA) were associated with substantial proteotoxicity.
evidence: This is supported by viability data in Figure 2D showing significant toxicity with NLS-GA65-GFP.

claim: Nuclear poly-GA formed aggregates at sites that were distinct from nucleoli, similar to the localization of poly-GA aggregates observed in patient brain.
source: Nuclear poly-GA formed aggregates at sites that were distinct from nucleoli, similar to the localization of poly-GA aggregates observed in patient brain (Schludi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 2B and citation (Schludi et al., 2015).

claim: Formation of nuclear poly-GA inclusions altered the shape of nucleoli as a result of mislocalization and partial sequestration of NPM1.
source: However, formation of these inclusions altered the shape of nucleoli as a result of mislocalization and partial sequestration of the abundant GC protein NPM1, consistent with the nucleolar abnormalities reported in neurons from C9orf72 cases (Mizielinska et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 2A and citation (Mizielinska et al., 2017).

claim: The nucleolar alterations caused by nuclear poly-GA are consistent with nucleolar abnormalities reported in neurons from C9orf72 cases.
source: However, formation of these inclusions altered the shape of nucleoli as a result of mislocalization and partial sequestration of the abundant GC protein NPM1, consistent with the nucleolar abnormalities reported in neurons from C9orf72 cases (Mizielinska et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference connecting experimental observations with cited patient data (Mizielinska et al., 2017).

claim: The inhibitory effect of nuclear poly-GA on nucleolar quality control was comparable to that previously observed for positively charged DPRs.
source: This inhibitory effect was comparable to that previously observed for positively charged DPRs, such as poly-PR, which accumulate directly within the GC phase of the nucleolus (Frottin et al., 2019; Mizielinska et al., 2017; Tao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference comparing current results with cited literature (Frottin et al., 2019; Mizielinska et al., 2017; Tao et al., 2015).

claim: R-DPRs apparently do not accumulate in the nucleolus in patient brain.
source: However, R-DPRs apparently do not accumulate in the nucleolus in patient brain (Mackenzie et al., 2015; Schludi et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations (Mackenzie et al., 2015; Schludi et al., 2015).

claim: R-DPRs may interfere with nucleolar quality control by a mechanism similar to that described for nuclear poly-GA.
source: and thus may rather interfere with nucleolar quality control by the mechanism described here for nuclear poly-GA (Frottin et al., 2019; Kwon et al., 2014; White et al., 2019).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential mechanisms in patients based on experimental observations and citations (Frottin et al., 2019; Kwon et al., 2014; White et al., 2019).

claim: Expression of poly-GA from G4C2-containing constructs resulted in substantially greater toxicity than expression from synthetic constructs when similar poly-GA lengths and amounts were compared.
source: Expression of poly-GA from G4C2-containing constructs resulted in substantially greater toxicity than expression from synthetic constructs when similar poly-GA lengths and amounts were compared.
evidence: This is supported by viability data in Figure 6A and expression level data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The G4C2 hexanucleotide repeat is thought to exert toxic effects in part by forming higher-order RNA assemblies in the nucleus that sequester RNA-binding proteins.
source: The G4C2 hexanucleotide repeat is thought to exert toxic effects in part by forming higher-order RNA assemblies in the nucleus that sequester RNA-binding proteins (Almeida et al., 2013; Cooper-Knock et al., 2015; Cooper-Knock et al., 2014; Donnelly et al., 2013; Haeusler et al., 2014; Mori et al., 2013b; Reddy et al., 2013; Rossi et al., 2015; Sareen et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Almeida et al., 2013; Cooper-Knock et al., 2015; Cooper-Knock et al., 2014; Donnelly et al., 2013; Haeusler et al., 2014; Mori et al., 2013b; Reddy et al., 2013; Rossi et al., 2015; Sareen et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2013).

claim: Longer G4C2 sequences may mediate additional effects.
source: Even if longer G4C2 sequences may mediate additional effects (West et al., 2020)
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on citation (West et al., 2020).

claim: The G4C2 constructs tested resulted in a pronounced inhibition of protein synthesis, even when coding for cytoplasmic poly-GA protein (NES-GA65).
source: the G4C2 constructs tested here resulted in a pronounced inhibition of protein synthesis, even when coding for cytoplasmic poly-GA protein (NES-GA65), which did not impair protein biogenesis when produced from a synthetic (non-G4C2) construct.
evidence: This is supported by OPP incorporation data in Figure 5D-E comparing NES-(G4C2)73-GFP with NES-GA65-GFP.

claim: Cytoplasmic poly-GA produced from synthetic constructs did not impair protein biogenesis.
source: the G4C2 constructs tested here resulted in a pronounced inhibition of protein synthesis, even when coding for cytoplasmic poly-GA protein (NES-GA65), which did not impair protein biogenesis when produced from a synthetic (non-G4C2) construct.
evidence: This is supported by OPP incorporation data in Figure 5D-E showing no effect of NES-GA65-GFP on protein synthesis.

claim: Expression constructs based on G4C2 repeats generate different RAN translation DPR products.
source: However, because expression constructs based on G4C2 repeats also generate the different RAN translation DPR products, a clear distinction between RNA and DPR toxicity in previous studies had been difficult.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RAN translation from G4C2 repeats.

claim: A clear distinction between RNA and DPR toxicity in previous studies had been difficult.
source: However, because expression constructs based on G4C2 repeats also generate the different RAN translation DPR products, a clear distinction between RNA and DPR toxicity in previous studies had been difficult.
evidence: This is an inference about limitations of prior research approaches.

claim: Expression of protein-only R-DPR constructs did not induce overt toxicity even when expressed at levels much higher than those generated by RAN translation of the G4C2 repeat.
source: Notably, expression of these protein-only constructs did not induce overt toxicity even when expressed at levels much higher than those generated by RAN translation of the G4C2 repeat.
evidence: This is supported by viability data in Figure 6A showing no toxicity of PR73-GFP and GR73-GFP, and immunoblot data in Figure 6B showing undetectable R-DPR production from G4C2 constructs.

claim: The major component of toxicity associated with G4C2 constructs can be unequivocally attributed to the production of the pathological G4C2 RNA sequence.
source: These findings allowed us to unequivocally attribute the major component of toxicity associated with G4C2 constructs to the production of the pathological G4C2 RNA sequence.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined observations that G4C2 constructs are highly toxic (Figure 6A), R-DPRs alone are not toxic (Figure 6A), and R-DPRs are not detectably produced from G4C2 constructs (Figure 6B).

claim: DPRs may be undetectable in the brain regions most affected by neurodegeneration in C9orf72 patients.
source: Although DPRs may be undetectable in the brain regions most affected by neurodegeneration in C9orf72 patients (Schludi et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation (Schludi et al., 2015).

claim: A DPR contribution to pathology in carriers of G4C2 expansions cannot be excluded.
source: we cannot exclude a DPR contribution to pathology in carriers of G4C2 expansions, where combinations of the various DPRs and mRNA are present simultaneously, and nondividing cells are exposed to these factors for extended time periods.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning acknowledging that patient conditions differ from the experimental model.

claim: Nuclear poly-GA interfered with protein biosynthesis, presumably by impairing the nucleolar function in ribosome biogenesis.
source: Indeed, nuclear poly-GA also interfered with protein biosynthesis, presumably by impairing the nucleolar function in ribosome biogenesis, and thus could enhance the toxic effects of G4C2 repeat RNA.
evidence: This is supported by OPP incorporation data in Figure 5D-E and is an inference about the mechanism based on nucleolar quality control data in Figure 2C.

claim: Nuclear poly-GA could enhance the toxic effects of G4C2 repeat RNA.
source: Indeed, nuclear poly-GA also interfered with protein biosynthesis, presumably by impairing the nucleolar function in ribosome biogenesis, and thus could enhance the toxic effects of G4C2 repeat RNA.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the additive effects observed in Figure 5D-E.

claim: The G4C2 expansion in C9orf72 interferes with multiple nuclear functions, culminating in an inhibition of protein biogenesis.
source: In summary, our results indicate that the G4C2 expansion in C9orf72 interferes with multiple nuclear functions, culminating in an inhibition of protein biogenesis, an outcome that would be especially harmful to neuronal cells.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on data showing effects on nucleolar quality control (Figure 2C), mRNA export (Figure 5A-B), and protein synthesis (Figure 5D-E).

claim: Inhibition of protein biogenesis would be especially harmful to neuronal cells.
source: In summary, our results indicate that the G4C2 expansion in C9orf72 interferes with multiple nuclear functions, culminating in an inhibition of protein biogenesis, an outcome that would be especially harmful to neuronal cells.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the implications for neurons based on general knowledge about neuronal vulnerability.

claim: These dominant toxic effects might be further aggravated by a loss of function of the endogenous C9ORF72 protein.
source: These dominant toxic effects might be further aggravated by a loss of function of the endogenous C9ORF72 protein, which is thought to play a role in cellular quality control (Boivin et al., 2020; Sellier et al., 2016; Sullivan et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on citations about C9ORF72 function (Boivin et al., 2020; Sellier et al., 2016; Sullivan et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2020).

claim: The endogenous C9ORF72 protein is thought to play a role in cellular quality control.
source: These dominant toxic effects might be further aggravated by a loss of function of the endogenous C9ORF72 protein, which is thought to play a role in cellular quality control (Boivin et al., 2020; Sellier et al., 2016; Sullivan et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Boivin et al., 2020; Sellier et al., 2016; Sullivan et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2020).
